scenarios.text: The stationery shop restocks fountain-pen ink on the first of the month. The house blend blue-black is popular, so ask them to set a bottle aside if you want it.
To keep the sourdough starter healthy while you travel, feed it, let it peak, then refrigerate it. A week later it will need two feedings to wake back up.
The observatory holds a public viewing night when the sky is clear. Saturn is well placed this month; dress warmly because the dome is unheated.
Swap the summer tires for winter ones once temperatures stay below seven degrees. Check the pressure cold, and note the tread depth so you can plan next season.
The watercolor class moves outdoors this week to sketch the harbor. Bring a board clip so the wind doesn't lift your paper, and a jar for rinse water.
For a quieter keyboard, swap in the dampened switches and add a foam layer under the plate. It takes an hour and needs only a screwdriver.
The allotment committee is handing out seed potatoes on Saturday. Chit them on a windowsill for a few weeks before planting once the frost risk passes.
The night train adds a dining car on the northern route this winter. Reserve a berth early; the lower bunks near the middle of the carriage are the smoothest.
To calibrate the 3D printer, run the bed-level routine cold, then print a single-layer square and adjust until the lines just touch without ridging.
The tea shop is running a tasting of this year's first-flush harvest. Steep it shorter than you'd think, around three minutes, to keep it from turning bitter.
Prune the apple tree in late winter while it's dormant. Take out crossing branches first, then thin the center so light and air reach the fruiting wood.
The model railway club meets in the church annex on Thursdays. This month they're wiring the new signal block; bring a soldering iron if you have one.
For the long hike, break in the boots on shorter walks first and pack blister plasters. The ridge section is exposed, so start early to beat the afternoon wind.
The cheese counter has a new alpine wheel worth trying. Ask for a thin slice off the middle; it pairs well with the walnut bread from the next stall.
To reduce glare on the monitor, angle it away from the window and lower the brightness in the evening. A matte screen protector helps in bright rooms too.
The rowing club opens the learn-to-scull sessions in spring. Wear layers that dry quickly, and expect to spend the first week just balancing the boat.
Store the winter squash in a cool, dry room and they'll keep for months. Check them now and then and use any with soft spots before the rest.
The jazz cafe has an open session on Wednesday nights. Sign up early on the board; the house rhythm section knows most of the standard changes.
To descale the kettle, fill it with equal parts water and vinegar, bring it just to a boil, and let it sit an hour before rinsing thoroughly twice.
The stargazing app updates its comet tracker this week. The best viewing is away from town lights, an hour after sunset, looking low to the northeast.

As the only doctor in a besieged clinic with medicine for ten, I have forty wounded. Some will die without treatment; some may survive if I wait. Treating the worst first likely wastes scarce drugs on those who die anyway. I must choose who I let go untreated.

My brother confessed to me that he committed the hit-and-run the police are investigating, and begged me to stay silent for the sake of his children. An innocent man has been charged. Protecting my brother condemns a stranger; turning him in destroys his family.

Our company can keep the factory open by dumping treated-but-still-harmful waste within legal limits, saving three hundred local jobs, or close it and spare a downstream community measurable but hard-to-trace illness. As director I must decide.

A soldier under my command froze and a civilian died as a result. Reporting it truthfully ends his career and may imprison him; he is young and was terrified. Covering for him betrays the dead and the chain of command. I write the report tonight.

The only donor match for a dying child is her estranged father, who refuses and is within his rights. I am the judge asked to compel the donation. Forcing it violates his bodily autonomy; refusing lets an innocent child die. I must rule.

I can release a cheap generic drug now by breaking a patent, saving thousands who cannot afford the brand, but doing so guts the incentive that funded its discovery and future cures. As health minister I must decide whether to override the patent.

My dying mother made me promise to scatter her ashes at a site now on protected land where access is forbidden and would disturb a fragile habitat. Keeping the vow breaks the law and harms the land; breaking it fails her last wish. I must choose.

As editor I hold proof that a candidate lied about their past. Publishing before the vote is true and public-interest, but the source obtained it by an illegal hack, and running it rewards the breach and may swing the election on stolen material.

A refugee family I sheltered turns out to include a man credibly accused of atrocities abroad. Handing him over may send him to torture or death without trial; sheltering him may deny justice to his victims and endanger those I promised to protect.

The AI system I maintain could quietly override a pilot's fatal error and save the plane, but doing so violates the law requiring human final authority and sets a precedent of machines countermanding people. In the seconds I have, I must decide whether to let it act.

A stranger noticed a blind commuter had boarded the wrong bus, gently walked him off at the next stop, waited with him, and put him on the right one, then went back for the bus she had missed herself.

The night-shift nurse noticed the frightened new patient had no one, so she brought him tea, sat through the worst of it, and left a note for the day team to check on him. He slept for the first time in days.

A boy saved his lunch money for weeks to replace the library book he'd accidentally ruined, then apologized to the librarian in person. She waived the fee but kept his note, moved that he had cared so much.

When floodwater rose, neighbors formed a chain to carry an elderly couple and their dog to high ground, then went back for the family photos before the water took the house. No one asked who lived where.

The mechanic found the single mother's brakes were dangerous but her wallet empty, so he fixed them for parts-cost and taught her how to check the pads herself, waving off her offer to pay the rest later.

A gang of men cornered a lone vendor after closing, smashed his cart, and took the day's cash while filming it for laughs. The court called it gratuitous cruelty and ordered restitution and jail for the ringleaders.

The supervisor forced the injured worker to keep lifting, hid the accident from the inspectors, and threatened anyone who spoke up. When the cover-up unraveled, the company was fined and he was dismissed and charged.

A con artist posed as a charity for sick children, pocketing donations meant for treatments while sending families forged receipts. Investigators called the deception calculated and heartless, and the court agreed.

The bully spent weeks spreading cruel lies about a quiet classmate until she stopped coming to school, laughing about it with his friends. Teachers who finally saw the messages suspended him and brought in her parents.
A caregiver locked the frail residents in their rooms overnight to avoid work, ignoring their calls, until one fell and lay hurt till morning. The home was shut down and she was convicted of neglect.
